docs/architecture.md
docs/graph-first-summarization-roadmap.md
features.acceptance:
- All three docs clearly state the three-part mission.
- A reader can understand from `before-you-start.md` alone what the system is for and what is still missing.
- The golden standard's purpose (integration oracle) is documented in the roadmap.

features.title: Fix strict typing defects in graph optimization
features.description: Repair the verified TypeScript type errors in the graph optimization layer so the optimization pipeline compiles cleanly under the project's strict compile gate. The known issue is that GraphOptimizationDelta values are passed through omitUndefinedDelta using a Record<string, unknown> constraint that is not accepted by TypeScript in the current implementation. The feature is complete when strict compilation passes for the optimization code without loosening the project's type-safety standards.
features.plan: Inspect graphOptimizer.ts and related types, determine whether GraphOptimizationDelta should satisfy the helper signature or whether the helper should be generalized, then implement the minimal type-safe fix and re-run strict compile verification and relevant optimization tests.
features.acceptance: Strict compile check passes for src/optimization/graphOptimizer.ts and related paths, and optimization tests still reflect the intended behavior after the type-safe fix.

features.title: Reconcile golden-standard pipeline output with documented graph-first behavior
features.description: Audit and reconcile the current pipeline outputs against the documented golden standard and graph-first architecture. Verified mismatches include root-style hierarchy and IDs instead of hand-authored semantic groupings, heuristic graph nodes/edges/provenance instead of the richer hand-authored graph snapshot, and downstream search/navigation/viewer surface differences. The work must classify each mismatch as a true implementation gap, a stale golden oracle, or documentation drift, and then converge the codebase on one explicit contract.
features.plan: Trace the strategy path, graph extraction path, graph snapshot derivation, and navigation/viewer surfaces against the docs-backed oracle. For each mismatch, decide whether the implementation must be brought to the current golden fixture, the golden fixture should be updated to the newer graph-first behavior, or the docs must be amended to explicitly bless the new contract. Preserve a remediation matrix and verify the chosen contract with targeted integration tests.
features.acceptance: There is a verified, doc-aligned contract for the golden fixture pack; the associated level, graph, search, navigation, and viewer integration tests either pass against that contract or are explicitly documented as known gaps with rationale.

features.title: Resolve inconsistent optimization goldens and stale documented deltas
features.description: Reconcile optimization expectations so the golden standard remains a trustworthy oracle. This includes fixing or explicitly re-authoring inconsistent expected deltas in the hand-authored golden surfaces, validating the intended optimizer math against the docs-backed contract, and refreshing any 'documented current delta' assertions that have gone stale. The goal is to ensure optimization failures clearly indicate implementation regressions rather than contradictions inside the golden fixtures.
features.plan: Compare graphOptimizer.ts behavior against the documented optimization intent and all optimization expectations stored in golden-surfaces.json and related tests. Identify where the implementation is wrong, where the golden data is self-contradictory, and where a known-gap assertion simply needs refreshing. Update the remediation matrix so optimization verification becomes reliable before broader golden-standard closure.
features.acceptance: Optimization expectations are internally consistent, documented delta assertions reflect the current intended gap set, and remaining optimization test failures—if any—clearly map to real code defects rather than stale or contradictory fixture data.

features.title: Increase graph extraction fidelity for golden-standard semantic grouping
features.description: Improve the logical-piece extraction and graph-building fidelity enough for the golden fixture to produce meaningful graph-derived communities and hand-authored-like semantic structure without relying on folder-first fallback. The immediate target is the order-workflow golden fixture, where current heuristic extraction under-produces relationships needed for graph-derived grouping and downstream surface alignment.
features.plan: Audit the golden fixture graph expectations against current extracted logicalDependencies, identify the missing dependency classes that materially affect community formation and flow derivation, and implement the smallest graph-fidelity improvements that let graph-derived L2/L3 grouping reflect meaningful project structure. Re-run graph, level, and surface integration tests to confirm whether fallback is avoided or remains an explicitly documented known gap.
features.acceptance: For the golden fixture, graph-derived grouping has enough semantic signal to avoid meaningless root-only fallback unless that fallback is explicitly documented as the intended contract, and downstream hierarchy-dependent surfaces reflect the agreed graph-first behavior.

features.title: Normalize optimization delta serialization and comparison contract
features.description: Define and implement a consistent contract for how GraphOptimizationDelta values are materialized, serialized, and compared in tests and golden fixtures. Optional delta fields that are not applicable for a given optimization suggestion should either be omitted consistently or normalized consistently, and the chosen rule must work with strict typing and with golden-surface verification. The goal is to prevent false mismatches caused by undefined-field shape differences while preserving the actual optimization meaning.
features.plan: Inspect GraphOptimizationDelta usage across optimizer code and tests, decide whether deltas should be structurally sparse or normalized to explicit keys, update the code and/or assertions to follow one contract, and verify that remaining optimization failures reflect semantic differences rather than serialization artifacts.
features.acceptance: GraphOptimizationDelta output follows one explicit serialization/comparison contract under strict typing, and optimization golden comparisons no longer fail solely because of omitted-versus-undefined field shape differences.

features.title: Broaden navigation search surfaces to graph-backed knowledge fields
features.description: Expand text search so navigation surfaces can discover items through graph-backed knowledge, not just literal names and descriptions. Candidate searchable fields include summary text, file path metadata, logical piece names and operations, dependency types, flow purpose text, and other graph-derived semantics already attached to the knowledge model. The goal is to make search behavior consistent with the graph-first intent and reduce golden-surface mismatches caused by overly narrow matching.
features.plan: Inventory the fields currently available on LevelItem metadata and ProjectKnowledge graph snapshots, define a stable search contract for text matching and scoring, then extend KnowledgeNavigator.searchByText (or add a richer search layer) to include the most valuable graph-backed fields. Reconcile the updated search behavior with the golden fixture expectations and document any remaining intentional deltas.
features.acceptance: Text search can match relevant items through richer graph-backed knowledge fields in addition to name/description, and search-related golden expectations reflect the agreed contract rather than shallow incidental matching.

features.title: Capture intra-file call edges in heuristic logical graph extraction
features.description: Extend heuristic logical-piece extraction so it can infer at least basic intra-project function call edges from source text, starting with same-file and imported-function call patterns that are present in the golden order-workflow fixture. This should enrich the graph snapshot with behavior-level relationships needed for better flow inference, signal quality, and graph-derived semantic grouping without relying solely on module import edges.
features.plan: Map extracted function names to logical pieces, inspect import bindings and call expressions that can be recognized deterministically, and emit call dependencies when a call target can be resolved to a known local logical piece. Start with the minimal patterns required for the golden fixture, then generalize carefully to avoid noisy false positives. Re-run graph snapshot and integration tests to confirm improved parity with the hand-authored oracle.
features.acceptance: For the golden fixture and similar simple projects, the heuristic graph extraction includes resolvable call edges between internal logical pieces, and downstream graph/flow surfaces become measurably closer to the hand-authored golden graph.

features.title: Reconcile graph signal taxonomy between docs, implementation, and golden fixtures
features.description: Align the graph signal contract across documentation, implementation, and golden fixtures so graph verification compares like with like. Decide whether orchestrator should become a formal signal kind, remain only a flow role, or be represented through another documented mechanism, then update the code/golden/docs accordingly. The goal is to prevent false graph mismatches caused by taxonomy drift while preserving the graph-first semantics the golden standard is meant to validate.
features.plan: Compare the signal kinds promised in the docs, the signals emitted by projectGraph.ts, the flow-role taxonomy used during path classification, and the hand-authored golden graph expectations. Choose one explicit contract and update the golden graph and/or implementation to follow it, with tests that keep signal and flow semantics distinct.
features.acceptance: Signal kinds and flow roles are explicitly distinguished or intentionally unified by a documented contract, and the golden graph no longer disagrees with the implementation solely because of taxonomy mismatch.

features.title: Enforce explicit unit-vs-integration test boundaries in scripts and Vitest config
features.description: The audit and runner-noise trace exposed that the repository does not currently enforce the intended testing contract: `npm run test` should execute only self-contained unit tests, while integration tests should be isolated under `tests/integration/` and executed only via `npm run test:integration`. This feature should make those boundaries explicit in repository scripts/config so tooling cannot accidentally treat fixture corpus files under `tests/fixtures/**` as runnable tests and so default local/CI runs stay unit-only unless integration coverage is explicitly requested.
features.plan:
1. Restore any fixture corpus files deleted during tracing.
2. Split Vitest execution into explicit unit and integration entrypoints, preferably with separate config files or explicit includes.
3. Update `package.json` scripts so `test` runs only unit tests and `test:integration` runs only integration tests.
4. Keep fixture corpora excluded from Vitest discovery.
5. Verify both commands independently and confirm the full contract is documented by the repo configuration.
features.acceptance: `npm run test` executes only unit tests, `npm run test:integration` executes only tests under `tests/integration/`, fixture files under `tests/fixtures/**` are never treated as runnable tests by repo config, and the split is verified by test runs.

features.title: Restore semantic golden-pack hierarchy via level overrides instead of root-style fallback
features.description: The audit established that the golden hand-authored pack is intentionally semantic: one `orders` feature inside one `order-workflow` module. The current passing test state was achieved by converging some expectations to root-style graph-derived fallback (`l2__root` / `l3__root`), but the documented contract in `docs/golden-standard-contract.md` explicitly says the golden pack should preserve semantic grouping via `levelOverrides` rather than downgrade the oracle to folder-root hierarchy. This remaining gap should be closed by making the integration path exercise the semantic override contract and by restoring the golden surfaces/pack expectations to those semantic IDs and ancestry relationships.
features.plan:
1. Re-read `docs/golden-standard-contract.md` and the golden pack integration setup.
2. Update the fixture generation path so the golden pack test runs with semantic `levelOverrides` (or equivalent explicit semantic grouping hook) instead of relying on generic root fallback.
3. Restore golden surfaces and pack expectations to `l2_orders` / `l3_order_workflow` and verify search/navigation/viewer ancestry remain coherent.
4. Run targeted integration tests and full suite to ensure the semantic contract is preserved without regressions.
features.acceptance: The golden pack integration path uses semantic grouping for the hand-authored fixture, producing `l2_orders` / `l3_order_workflow` (or an explicitly documented equivalent), and docs/tests/fixtures all agree on that contract.

features.title: Redesign the viewer information architecture around a project-first inspection workflow
features.description: Replace the current viewer's implementation-driven navigation and sidebar controls with a project-first inspection workflow that matches the intended golden-standard contract. The user should select an existing project or enter a new path, land on an Overview tab first, and then inspect the project through coherent surfaces rather than internal pipeline toggles. The redesign must remove or hide misleading controls such as 'Use LLM for summaries', 'Use graph-derived map (L2/L3)', and direct optimization objective selectors from the default inspection flow, because these expose implementation details that the user cannot meaningfully reason about. Instead, the viewer should present project readiness, inspection surfaces, and explicit follow-up actions such as requesting additional LLM summary passes.
features.plan:
1. Audit the current viewer tab set, sidebar controls, and API shape in `viewer/index.html` and `viewer/serve.ts`.
2. Define the target information architecture: project picker -> Overview -> Tree -> Graph -> Search -> Improvements -> Decisions -> Metrics -> Runs -> Detail, with Overview as the landing tab.
3. Replace implementation-centric controls with user-facing actions and statuses, preserving advanced controls only behind an explicit review/debug affordance if still needed.
4. Update the viewer contract docs and the small-clean golden surfaces to reflect the new Overview-first workflow.
5. Add regression tests that lock the presence/absence of the intended tabs and sidebar controls.
features.acceptance:
- The viewer lands on an Overview tab after project selection rather than Tree.
- The default sidebar flow is project selection plus user-facing summary actions, not raw implementation toggles.
- The primary inspection workflow no longer exposes 'Use LLM for summaries', 'Use graph-derived map (L2/L3)', or raw optimization objective controls in the main user path.
- Regression tests verify the intended tabs/controls contract.

features.title: Add an Overview readiness surface and unify user-facing run reporting
features.description: Introduce a first-class Overview surface that answers the user's primary inspection questions before they drill into tree, graph, search, or detail. The Overview must show whether the project has been summarised, whether the graph and other required processing stages have completed, whether the project is ready for inspection, and what additional summaries can still be requested. It must also collapse the current extraction-vs-summary split into a single user-facing run history/pipeline view that reports overall pass status, duration, and cost, while still preserving stage-level data for diagnostics behind the scenes.
features.plan:
1. Replace the current lightweight status-pill strip with a real Overview tab and readiness model.
2. Define explicit readiness criteria from the existing data returned by `viewer/serve.ts`: levels present, graph present, summaries present, optimization computed, and any other required stages.
3. Add a unified run summary that combines extraction and summary activity into a single user-facing pass record with timing and cost, while preserving lower-level telemetry for debug surfaces.
4. Extend the API payload as needed to expose total cost and consolidated run metadata.
5. Add regression tests for Overview readiness states and the single-pass run presentation contract.
features.acceptance:
- The viewer contains an Overview tab that is the primary landing surface after project selection.
- Overview states whether the project is ready for inspection and which required stages are complete or missing.
- The user-facing run history is presented as a unified pass with duration and cost rather than separate extraction and summary concepts.
- Regression tests lock the readiness and unified-run contract.

features.title: Replace level-by-level graph views with a unified multi-level hierarchy graph
features.description: Rework the graph surface so the user can see the whole project hierarchy and its interactions in one graph rather than switching between isolated level-specific views. The target contract is a unified graph that shows L1 nodes directly, groups them into visible L2 circles or clusters, groups those into L3, and then groups those into L4/project-system scope. The user must be able to toggle levels on and off inside this single graph rather than switching between separate graph tabs or dropdown-selected single-level graphs. This is required both for truthful inspection of project structure and for verifying that the golden slug-ify hierarchy behaves correctly as one system.
features.plan:
1. Audit the current graph endpoint and D3 rendering path, which currently loads one level at a time via `/graph?level=`.
2. Define a payload that includes cross-level hierarchy, group membership, and dependency edges needed for unified rendering.
3. Implement a nested/grouped graph view that can render all levels together and allow per-level visibility toggles.
4. Update the small-clean golden surfaces to describe the expected unified graph structure and controls.
5. Add regression tests for the unified graph contract and removal of single-level-only dependence in the main workflow.
features.acceptance:
- The viewer can render all relevant hierarchy levels together in one graph.
- L1 nodes are visually grouped into L2, L2 into L3, and L3 into L4/project-system scope.
- Users can toggle visible levels on/off inside the unified graph.
- The golden viewer contract includes expectations for the unified graph behavior.

features.title: Clarify search scoring and make search results explainable in the viewer
features.description: Audit and tighten the viewer's search surface so result scoring is understandable and contractually meaningful. Today the percentage-like score shown in results is unclear because the underlying text search uses weighted match scores such as 1, 0.6, and 0.5 across names, descriptions, summaries, metadata, logical pieces, signals, dependency types, and flows. The viewer must stop presenting this as an unexplained percentage and instead either display a clearly named score/confidence with explanation, or provide per-result reasons showing which graph-backed fields matched. This work should also ensure the search surface remains aligned with graph-backed knowledge rather than shallow label matching alone.
features.plan:
1. Trace the current scoring logic in `KnowledgeNavigator.searchByText` and how it is rendered in the viewer.
2. Define a user-facing contract for score display: e.g. 'match score', 'matched in summary and flow purpose', or another explainable representation.
3. Extend the search API/result model if needed so the viewer can render match reasons, not just a number.
4. Update the small-clean golden surfaces and regression tests to lock the agreed search explanation behavior.
features.acceptance:
- Search results no longer display an unexplained percentage-like value.
- The viewer explains result scoring or match reasons in user-facing terms.
- Regression tests cover the search score/explanation contract.

features.title: Replace obsolete Improvements view with graph-optimization inspection surfaces
features.description: Retire the current Improvements tab contract and replace it with viewer surfaces that expose the project's agreed graph-optimization model. Instead of an obsolete or generic improvements list, this area should show optimization proposals derived from the graph contract: the ideal graph for different objectives, scoped vs global optimization suggestions, expected deltas, trade-offs, and the rationale for why a change improves dependency count, flow hops, latency, memory, or other agreed metrics. The viewer should therefore become a trustworthy inspection surface for the same optimization contract that the golden standard validates.
features.plan:
1. Audit the current Improvements tab and the optimization data available from `graphOptimizer.ts` / viewer APIs.
2. Define the user-facing optimization inspection model: current graph state, objective selection, suggested changes, delta summary, trade-offs, and evidence.
3. Remove or repurpose obsolete UI elements that no longer reflect the perfect-graph optimization contract.
4. Update golden surfaces/tests so the Improvements tab is validated against the graph-optimization model rather than the old placeholder behavior.
features.acceptance:
- The Improvements tab is backed by the graph optimization contract rather than the old placeholder behavior.
- Users can inspect optimization proposals, deltas, and rationale for agreed objectives.
- Golden/viewer regression tests validate the new Improvements surface.

features.title: Define and enforce a clean user-facing Detail tab contract
features.description: Redesign the Detail tab so it becomes the cleanest and most informative project-inspection surface instead of a metadata dump. The user-facing contract must exclude raw metadata and instead show only the final understanding of what a selected item is, what it does, how it relates to the rest of the project, and why it matters. This includes eliminating duplicate/degenerate hierarchy presentation, ensuring standard files such as `package.json` and `src/index.js` receive meaningful explanations, and making the Detail view faithfully reflect the reviewed L1-L4 slug-ify hierarchy rather than leaking implementation-era placeholders.
features.plan:
1. Audit the current Detail rendering path and identify which metadata sections should be removed or hidden from the default user-facing view.
2. Define the target Detail schema: one-line summary, fuller explanation, role in project/system, incoming/outgoing relationships, relevant flow/context, and optional review/debug evidence behind an explicit affordance.
3. Add coverage for standard-files explanations (`package.json`, `index.js`) and for eliminating duplicated L2/L3 presentation where the hierarchy is degenerate.
4. Update the small-clean golden surfaces/tests so Detail becomes a contractually verified user-facing surface rather than an incidental dump.
features.acceptance:
- The default Detail tab shows user-facing understanding rather than raw metadata.
- `package.json`, `index.js`, and other important files have meaningful explanations in the slug-ify golden contract.
- The Detail surface no longer presents degenerate duplicated hierarchy as if it were meaningful.
- Regression tests lock the Detail contract.

features.title: Create a slug-ify golden review workspace with raw outputs and reviewer comments
features.description: Add a review workflow around the small `slug-ify` fixture so the golden standard can be iterated hand in hand with the viewer. For every reviewed piece across L4/L3/L2/L1, the user should be able to inspect the final user-facing rendering, the underlying raw outputs/evidence that produced it, and a place to record reviewer comments while converging on the true golden contract. This workspace should also allow the same reviewed data to drive the tree, graph, search, and detail surfaces so the viewer can be validated directly against the audited golden standard rather than against incidental live output alone.
features.plan:
1. Define the review artifact model for small-clean: reviewed hierarchy expectations, raw extraction/summarization evidence, current rendered surface output, reviewer comments, and approval state.
2. Decide whether comments live in new fixture-side JSON files, `.factory` artifacts, or another review pack format.
3. Extend the viewer and/or supporting APIs so a reviewer can inspect raw output alongside final output for each piece and add comments during golden convergence.
4. Add regression coverage ensuring the review workspace can render the reviewed slug-ify golden pack and its linked tree/graph/detail/search surfaces.
features.acceptance:
- There is a repository-backed review workspace/artifact model for the small-clean golden pack.
- A reviewer can inspect raw outputs and final outputs for each L4/L3/L2/L1 piece and record comments.
- The same reviewed data can be used to validate viewer surfaces such as tree, graph, search, and detail.

features.title: Define the reviewed slug-ify L4/L3/L2/L1 hierarchy contract and fix degenerate grouping
features.description: Produce and enforce an explicit reviewed hierarchy contract for the small `slug-ify` (`small-clean`) fixture, covering what should appear at L4, L3, L2, and L1 and why. The current pipeline/viewer shape is degenerate for review purposes because L2 and L3 are effectively the same folder buckets (`root`, `src`, `tests`), while L4 is generated only as a minimal synthetic wrapper and is not part of the main project payload or viewer workflow. This feature should therefore define and lock the reviewed semantic hierarchy already indicated by the fixture files and hand-authored graph: L4 as the `slug-ify` project/system; L3 as meaningful areas such as public library surface, text transformation engine, and verification; L2 as package/runtime wiring, public API entrypoint, slug creation, slug restoration, shared text-normalization helpers, and focused test areas; and L1 as the concrete files under those areas. The result should explain where `package.json`, `src/index.js`, implementation files, and tests belong in the system and prevent the golden standard from accepting duplicated hierarchy as meaningful structure.
features.plan:
1. Audit the current `small-clean` golden surfaces, stage1 graph, dependency snapshot, tests, and live `generateLevels`/`generateL4` behavior.
2. Replace the current duplicate folder-bucket expectation with the reviewed semantic hierarchy matrix for `slug-ify`.
3. Decide which parts require implementation changes, which require golden fixture updates, and which require explicit level overrides or a graph-derived grouping strategy.
4. Update docs/goldens/tests so degenerate duplicated L2/L3 hierarchy is no longer treated as an acceptable oracle for the reviewed fixture, and so L4 becomes a first-class part of the reviewed contract.
features.acceptance:
- The small-clean fixture has an explicit reviewed L4/L3/L2/L1 contract.
- The contract explains the role of `package.json`, `src/index.js`, implementation files, and tests within the overall system.
- The reviewed hierarchy is semantic rather than duplicated folder buckets.
- Golden tests/docs/viewer expectations distinguish true semantic hierarchy from accidental filesystem grouping.

features.title: Add viewer regression coverage for the reviewed golden contract surfaces
features.description: Add explicit regression coverage for the viewer-facing contract so passing backend/golden tests are no longer mistaken for proof that the inspection experience is correct. The current audit verified that the viewer can still be materially wrong even while existing tests pass: it lands on Tree instead of Overview, exposes implementation toggles in the primary workflow, renders single-level graph views, shows opaque search percentages, splits runs into extraction vs summary, and leaks raw metadata/debug data into Detail. This feature should create durable viewer regression tests around the reviewed small-clean golden contract so the project can detect those divergences automatically.
features.plan: Created tests/integration/viewerGoldenContract.test.ts with 62 regression tests across 7 describe blocks covering all six viewer contract failure modes identified in the feature description. All 62 tests pass; full integration suite (206 tests) is green.
features.acceptance: tests/integration/viewerGoldenContract.test.ts exists with passing tests for all six viewer surfaces. Running vitest.integration.config.ts confirms 206/206 pass.

features.title: Viewer: Cache-first project loading — skip re-analysis if data already exists
features.description: When a project is selected that already has a completed analysis result (server-side cache hit), load and display it immediately without showing the loading overlay or re-running the pipeline. Add a clearly labelled 'Re-run analysis' button (or refresh icon) in the actions sidebar so the user can force a fresh pass on demand. The loading overlay and progress bar should only appear for genuine first-run or forced-refresh scenarios. The server-side cache key already covers this; the fix is on the client: detect the cacheHit flag in the response and suppress the unnecessary loading UX, and provide a separate explicit reload action.
features.plan:
1. On loadProject(), start progress polling and show the overlay only if the first response is NOT a cache hit.
2. After receiving the initial response, check analysisMeta.cacheHit — if true, skip overlay and render immediately.
3. Add a 'Re-run analysis' button to the actions sidebar that clears the server-side cache for the current preset (new /api/project/:id/invalidate endpoint) and then calls loadProject().
4. Update the actions sidebar copy to distinguish 'Re-run analysis' from 'Request LLM summary pass'.
features.acceptance:
- Selecting a project that was analysed in the same session renders instantly with no loading overlay.
- A 'Re-run analysis' button is present and forces a fresh pipeline run.
- Loading overlay only appears for genuine first-run or forced-refresh.
- The analysisMeta.cacheHit flag is used server-side and surfaced to the client.

features.title: Viewer Overview: remove 'Inspection surfaces' card grid — it duplicates the top tabs
features.description: Remove the 'Inspection surfaces' card grid from the Overview tab entirely. The top tab bar already provides all the same navigation. The Overview should focus only on project-level status: readiness checklist, quality score, hierarchy summary, and optionally a brief prose description of next steps — no redundant navigation tiles.
features.plan:
1. Locate the 'Inspection surfaces' section in renderOverview() in viewer/index.html.
2. Delete that section entirely.
3. Optionally add a short contextual paragraph at the bottom of Overview pointing users to specific tabs if needed (text, not tiles).
4. Verify no other code depends on those card onclick='switchTab(...)' calls within Overview.
features.acceptance:
- The Overview tab does not render the 'Inspection surfaces' card grid.
- The top tab bar is the only navigation mechanism between surfaces.
- Overview content is: readiness checklist, quality score, hierarchy summary.

features.title: Viewer: Remove verbose analysis status pills below the tabs
features.description: Remove the analysis-status pill strip that sits below the tab bar (the bar rendered by renderAnalysisStatus()). The same information is available in the Overview readiness section and the Runs/Metrics tabs. A permanently visible implementation telemetry bar makes the viewer feel like a debug tool rather than a project-knowledge browser. If any status indicator is still needed in the chrome at all, limit it to a single unobtrusive indicator — e.g. a small dot or badge on the Overview tab label — rather than a multi-pill bar on every panel.
features.plan:
1. Remove or hide the #analysis-status bar in the viewer HTML template.
2. Remove the call to renderAnalysisStatus() in loadProject().
3. If a minimal status indicator is still desired, add a small dot/badge to the Overview tab label only.
4. Verify that no other visible surface loses information that is not covered by Overview readiness or Runs/Metrics tabs.
context: Below the tab bar there is a row of status pills: 'Analysis: fresh-run', 'Run count: 1', 'Graph ready (N nodes, N edges, N flows)', 'Summaries ready (N items)', 'Extraction rows: N', 'Summary rows: N'.
This strip is technical telemetry that belongs in the Metrics or Runs tab — not in the primary chrome visible on every panel.
New users have no meaningful frame of reference for 'Extraction rows' or 'Summary rows'.
The Overview tab's 'Project Readiness' section already surfaces this information in human-readable form.
features.acceptance:
- The analysis-status pill strip is not visible below the tabs in the default viewer layout.
- The Overview readiness section still shows the same information in human-readable form.
- Runs/Metrics tabs retain all telemetry data for those who need it.

features.title: Tree: fix redundant label repetition — show what each item IS, not what its kind is
features.description:
Fix the Tree tab so each item row shows a meaningful one-line description of what the item IS and DOES, never a mechanical repetition of its name or kind. The fix has two parts:

1. **Renderer fix**: in `renderTree()`, the description shown next to each node must prefer `item.summary.summary` over `item.description` when the summary exists and is non-empty. Currently the renderer always uses `node.item.summary ? node.item.summary.summary : node.item.description`, which is correct logic but depends on summaries being populated — so the second fix is critical.

2. **Summarisation root cause**: the heuristic summarizer's fallback produces 'File: <path>' and 'Feature group from directory: <dir>' as descriptions. These should never appear as the user-visible summary in the tree. The `withFallbackSummary()` function in `levelGenerator.ts` must not promote these mechanical placeholders to `item.summary.summary`. Instead, when the LLM is not available and no real summary exists, the tree should show the raw `item.description` field (which may itself be a placeholder) but clearly signal that it is unreviewed, rather than copying the placeholder into the summary slot.
features.plan:
1. Read the tree render path in viewer/index.html to confirm how the description text is assembled.
2. Read withFallbackSummary() and the heuristic summarizer to understand exactly which strings end up in item.summary.summary.
3. Patch the fallback so that mechanical placeholder strings ('File: X', 'Feature group from directory: X', 'Module: X') are NOT promoted into the summary field — leave summary undefined/empty in those cases so the renderer can choose a fallback display strategy.
4. Update the tree renderer to show 'No summary yet' or a muted placeholder when no real summary is available, rather than silently copying the mechanical description.
5. Verify against small-clean golden-standard.json: when hand-authored descriptions are loaded via level overrides, they must appear verbatim in the tree.
context: In the Tree tab each row currently shows e.g. 'L1 package.json File: package.json' — the name is repeated as the description because the heuristic summary falls back to 'File: <path>'.
Similarly higher-level rows show 'L3 tests Module: tests' and 'L2 tests Feature group from directory: tests', where the description is just the kind + the name again, with no meaningful content.

The golden-standard.json for small-clean has hand-authored descriptions: 'Package manifest for the slug-ify fixture that declares module metadata, test script, and the public entry-point exposed via src/index.js.' These descriptions MUST be what the viewer shows.

The root cause is two-fold: (a) the item description is a generated placeholder (e.g. 'File: package.json') rather than a meaningful summary, and (b) the tree renderer does not pull from item.summary.summary even when a real summary exists.
features.acceptance:
- Tree rows for L1 items show a meaningful description, never 'File: <name>' or 'Module: <name>'.
- Tree rows for L2/L3 items show a meaningful description, never 'Feature group from directory: <dir>'.
- When no summary exists, the tree shows a clear 'No summary' indicator rather than a meaningless repeated label.
- The hand-authored descriptions from golden-standard.json appear correctly in the tree when loaded via level overrides.

features.title: Detail: wire hand-authored descriptions and graph piece data into the rendered view
features.description:
Fix the Detail panel so it shows genuinely useful information for every item — sourcing from the best available data in priority order: LLM/hand-authored summary — logical piece 'what' field (from golden-standard.json or LLM extraction) — item.description if meaningful — 'No description yet'.

Specifically:
1. The 'What (one line)' field must never show 'File: <path>', 'Module: <name>', or any other purely mechanical placeholder. If item.summary.summary is such a placeholder, fall through to the next source.
2. The 'Why (purpose)' field must not read 'Purpose inferred from item description: <repeated placeholder>'. If the summary.purpose is a generated fallback string, suppress it and look for the item's role in the hierarchy instead.
3. The 'How (composition & drill-down)' field must not show 'Fallback summary used because the model returned incomplete structured fields.' This string must never appear in the user-facing Detail; it is a debug artifact and should be logged, not rendered.
4. When a logical piece with confidence=1 (hand-authored) or high-confidence LLM provenance has a 'what' field, use that as the primary description source for L1 items.
5. The Detail for the small-clean slug-ify fixture should, after this fix, show the hand-authored descriptions from golden-standard.json and the golden-graph-stage1.json piece data for each file.
features.plan:
1. Read the Detail rendering path in viewer/index.html (renderDetail function) and identify all places where summary.summary, summary.purpose, and summary.keyResponsibilities are rendered.
2. Define a helper getItemWhat(item) that returns the best available one-line description, rejecting known mechanical placeholder patterns.
3. Define getItemWhy(item) that rejects 'Purpose inferred from item description:...' patterns and instead computes a role-in-system sentence from the hierarchy.
4. Define getItemHow(item) that rejects the fallback debug string and instead renders children, dependencies, or logical piece operations.
5. Apply these helpers in the Detail renderer.
6. Add at least one test in the viewer contract tests that asserts the fallback debug string never appears in a rendered Detail.
context:
Opening Detail for package.json currently shows:
  What (one line): 'File: package.json'
  Why (purpose): 'Purpose inferred from item description: File: package.json'
  How (composition & drill-down): 'Fallback summary used because the model returned incomplete structured fields.'
This is the most visible signal that summarisation has failed: the Detail view is the canonical place a user looks to understand a file.

The Golden Review panel shows the raw hand-authored piece for package.json with a rich 'what' field: 'Package manifest for the slug-ify fixture that declares module metadata, test script, and the public entry-point exposed via src/index.js.' and a full 'operations' list. This data already exists in the model and must reach the Detail view.

The root cause is (a) the heuristic summarizer never calls the LLM when no LLM is configured, so item.summary ends up as a purely mechanical fallback, and (b) the Detail renderer does not fall back to the logical piece 'what'/'operations' fields even when they are richer than the summary.

The Detail view must source from: first, item.summary.summary if it is a real LLM-generated or hand-authored sentence; second, the logical piece 'what' field if the piece has hand-authored/high-confidence provenance; third, the item.description if it is non-mechanical; finally a clear 'No description available' indicator.
features.acceptance:
- Detail for package.json in slug-ify shows the hand-authored description from golden-standard.json, not 'File: package.json'.
- The string 'Fallback summary used because the model returned incomplete structured fields.' never appears in rendered Detail HTML.
- The string 'Purpose inferred from item description:' never appears in rendered Detail HTML.
- If no meaningful information exists, Detail shows 'No description available' rather than a mechanical placeholder.
- Regression test added to viewerGoldenContract.test.ts covering these constraints.

features.title: Improvements tab: add a 'Flows' section that explains project flows in plain language
features.description:
Add a dedicated 'Flows' tab (or a prominent 'Flows' section within the Graph tab, or as the first section of Improvements) that:

1. Lists all inferred flows in the project by their human-readable name.
2. For each flow shows: name, brief description of what it does end-to-end, the sequence of items it passes through (L1 files / L2 features), and whether it has a perceivable output.
3. Uses plain language — no internal jargon. A user who does not know what a 'flow' is should be able to read the section and understand they are looking at 'the paths through which data or control travels in this project'.
4. Clearly distinguishes healthy flows (have input and output) from dead/orphan flows (no perceivable output — candidate for removal).
5. Links each flow step to the corresponding item in Tree/Detail so the user can navigate to the relevant file.

This should be a new top-level tab 'Flows' placed between 'Graph' and 'Improvements'.
features.plan:
1. Read the current graph data payload (serve.ts /api/project/:id/graph response) to see what flow data is returned.
2. Add a /api/project/:id/flows endpoint (or include flows in the existing graph response) that returns: flow id, name, description, nodes in sequence, whether output is present.
3. Add a 'Flows' tab to the viewer tab bar between Graph and Improvements.
4. Implement renderFlows() that renders the flow list as: header with flow name, prose description, step-by-step node list, status badge (healthy/dead), and clickable links to Detail for each step.
5. Update the golden-surfaces.json for small-clean to include the expected Flows tab content.
6. Add regression tests for the Flows tab presence and basic content shape.
context: The Improvements tab currently shows flow-related optimization suggestions that reference 'flows' as a concept, but a first-time user has no idea what a flow is.
The Graph tab shows nodes and edges but has no 'Flows' dimension surfaced as a named thing.
The golden-standard graph for slug-ify has two named flows: the slugify flow (input → utils → slugify → output) and the deslugify flow (input → utils → deslugify → output).

Flows are a first-class concept in the graph-first contract — every input must have an output, dead flows are removal candidates — but the viewer currently treats them as an internal technical detail rather than a user-facing concept.
features.acceptance:
- A 'Flows' tab exists between 'Graph' and 'Improvements' in the viewer.
- Each flow is listed with a human-readable name and end-to-end prose description.
- Each step in the flow links to the corresponding Detail view.
- Flows without a perceivable output are flagged as 'Dead flow — no output detected'.
- The slug-ify fixture shows at least the slugify and deslugify flows.
- Regression tests cover the Flows tab contract.

features.title: Iterative pipeline convergence toward the golden-standard.json hierarchy
features.description:
Design and execute an iterative convergence loop that brings the pipeline's automatic output for the slug-ify (small-clean) fixture as close as possible to the hand-authored golden-standard.json hierarchy, without requiring manual overrides.

**Core framing:** The golden-standard.json is the TARGET — the representation a correct, semantics-first pipeline should independently produce when it analyses slug-ify. The pipeline's job is to analyse the source files and emit something structurally and semantically equivalent. The golden file is not fed into the pipeline as a config; it is the oracle we measure against.

```
project source files
       ↓
  pipeline (extraction → grouping → summarisation → graph)
       ↓
  produced representation   ←→   golden-standard.json (target)
                               (diff = what still needs fixing)
```

The convergence loop has three phases per iteration:

**Phase 1: Measure the gap**
Run the current pipeline against small-clean. Produce a structured diff between the generated hierarchy (L4→L3→L2→L1) and the golden-standard.json target. For each golden item, state whether the pipeline produced a matching item (by semantic similarity, not just ID), at what level, with what description quality. Score on: correct level assignment, correct grouping (which L1 files are under which L2), correct L3 assignment, meaningful L4 description, and meaningful item descriptions.

**Phase 2: Root-cause the biggest gaps**
Trace each gap to the specific code path that produced the wrong output. The three most likely root causes are:
  - genericStrategy.generateL2() groups by directory — should use semantic cues from file content, imports, and logical piece types
  - genericStrategy.generateL3() groups by top-level directory — should use graph community structure or LLM-derived themes
  - heuristicSummarizer produces mechanical descriptions that are never close to the hand-authored ones

**Phase 3: Implement the smallest change that closes the biggest gap**
For each iteration, implement ONE change that moves the score closer to the target. Candidate improvements in priority order:
  1. Use import graph edges to infer feature co-location: if A imports B (especially if A is a test file), they belong in the same L2 group.
  2. Use logical piece graph signals (bridge, isolated-sink, isolated-source) to inform L2 grouping decisions.
  3. Use filename patterns and logical piece kinds to refine L2 names.
  4. Promote the logical piece 'what' field to item.description when it is more meaningful than 'File: X'.
  5. Use an LLM pass over L2/L3 grouping decisions when the heuristic score is below a threshold.

After each iteration, re-run the gap measurement and record the new score. Continue until either the pipeline score is above a defined threshold OR the remaining gaps are explicitly classified as 'requires LLM' and documented as known limitations.

**Concrete first iteration targets:**
- L2 grouping: group slugify.js and slugify.test.js together (currently split into l2_src and l2_tests). The golden has them in the same L2 feature.
- L3 grouping: produce at least 2 semantically meaningful L3 groups rather than folder-name buckets.
- L4: produce a meaningful project description rather than 'System: small-clean'.
- L1 descriptions: derive from logical piece 'what' field rather than 'File: <path>'.

**Note on the levelOverrides mechanism:** The existing `config.levelOverrides` mechanism can be used during development to force the correct grouping and verify that the rest of the pipeline (search, navigation, viewer) works correctly once grouping is right. But the long-term goal is the pipeline producing the right grouping autonomously — overrides are a scaffold for testing, not the solution.
features.plan:
Iteration 0 (baseline measurement):
1. Run generateLevels() against small-clean with persist=false.
2. Compare each generated item against golden-standard.json by file path (L1), by children set (L2/L3), and by description quality.
3. Produce a score matrix: for each golden item, score 0-3 on grouping correctness and 0-3 on description quality.
4. Record the baseline score.

Iteration 1 (L2 grouping by import co-location):
1. Modify generateL2() in genericStrategy to detect 'feature clusters': if two L1 files have a direct import edge between them AND the importer is a test file, co-locate them in the same L2 feature group instead of splitting by directory.
2. Re-run and re-score.

Iteration 2 (L1 descriptions from logical pieces):
1. In generateLevels(), after logical piece extraction, set item.description to the module piece's 'what' field (heuristic-extracted) when it is more meaningful than 'File: X'.
2. Re-run and re-score.

Iteration 3 (L3 grouping from graph community):
1. Build a simple graph community detector that uses the import edges to produce connected components. Use these components as L3 candidates instead of top-level directory names.
2. Re-run and re-score.

Iteration 4+ (LLM refinement):
If the heuristic score plateaus below threshold, introduce an optional LLM grouping pass. This pass should be optional and disabled by default, so the heuristic baseline is still tested independently.
features.acceptance:
- A structured gap measurement exists for the current pipeline output vs golden-standard.json, with a numerical score.
- At least 3 iterations have been completed, each with a documented score improvement.
- The pipeline correctly co-locates implementation and test files for the same feature in the same L2 group (without manual overrides).
- L1 item descriptions are derived from graph extraction logical piece 'what' fields rather than 'File: X' mechanical fallbacks.
- The gap measurement and iteration results are preserved in a companion file (e.g. docs/convergence-log.md or a fixture-side JSON) so future iterations can continue from the last known state.
- The pipeline changes are covered by at least one integration test that verifies the convergence score meets the defined threshold.

features.title: Critically audit and harden the hand-authored golden-standard.json for slug-ify
features.description:
Perform a focused critical audit of tests/fixtures/small-clean/golden-standard.json and produce an improved version that is internally consistent, semantically justified at every level, and usable as an unambiguous target for pipeline convergence.

This is NOT a code task — it is a thinking and editing task. The deliverable is a revised golden-standard.json that represents the ideal pipeline output for slug-ify: what a correct, semantics-first pipeline SHOULD produce if it analyses this project correctly. Getting this file right is the prerequisite for all pipeline convergence work — optimising toward a wrong target makes everything downstream suspect.

**Decisions made and applied across all three fixture golden files:**

1. **Hierarchy contract: L0–L4 all covered** — L4 = project/system, L3 = two semantic areas ('public surface', 'transformation engine'), L2 = feature groups, L1 = file or intra-file semantic unit with verified line numbers, L0 = individual exported/private function with exact lines. All three fixtures (small-clean, small-dirty-single, small-dirty) now follow this same hierarchy.

2. **Level skips are permitted and used** — `package.json` is a direct L1 child of L3 'public surface', skipping an intermediate L2 wrapper that adds no semantic value. Documented explicitly in each file's `contract.decisions` block.

3. **Test co-location decision** — Tests live inside the same L2 group as the implementation they verify. Rationale: proximity = context. If you want to understand `slugify.js`, you want its test immediately adjacent — not in a different area of the hierarchy.

4. **Naming convention** — Human-readable lowercase phrases only. No `snake_case`, no `_feature` suffixes. Names must make sense in isolation.

5. **Description format (all levels)** — Implementation-agnostic: true even if the code is rewritten. Conveys contract (what it guarantees), role (why it exists), and coupling cost (what breaks downstream if it changes). Does not repeat `path` or `lines` fields in prose. Does not say 'Called by X at line N'. L0 descriptions let a reader imagine the code without seeing it, but do not describe the implementation.

6. **Dependencies model** — Every item carries a `dependencies` array with `itemId` and `relationship` explaining the nature of coupling, not just 'imports' but what specifically breaks if the target changes its contract.

7. **Self-describing contract block** — Every golden file has a top-level `contract` object with `version`, `scope`, `fields` (what each key means), and `decisions` (explicit choices made).

8. **Semantic equivalence across fixtures** — Despite 18 source files in small-dirty, the genuine semantic structure is identical to small-clean: two public transforms backed by two shared text-normalisation helpers. All three fixtures produce structurally equivalent hierarchies. Differences are documented in each file's `decisions` block.

9. **Noise classification (small-dirty)** — 13 infrastructure classes (no-op pass-throughs, empty emitters) earn no L2+ representation. `utils.js` exports 26 functions; only 2 are output-affecting. `deslugify.js` imports 3 functions from utils.js that are never called (phantom imports — no real dependency). `slugify.js` instantiates 12 infrastructure classes; every method call is a no-op relative to return value.

10. **Line numbers in all three fixtures** — All L0 and L1 items carry verified `lines: [start, end]` ranges. For the monolith (small-dirty-single), all items share the same file path but have distinct line ranges. This is the correct representation for a monolith case.

**Files delivered:**
- `tests/fixtures/small-clean/golden-standard.json` — clean multi-file version, L0–L4, verified line numbers
- `tests/fixtures/small-dirty-single/golden-standard.json` — single-file monolith, same hierarchy, line-range-based L1/L0
- `tests/fixtures/small-dirty/golden-standard.json` — noisy multi-file, same semantic structure, explicit noise classification
features.plan: Delivered. All three fixture golden files revised.
context: The file tests/fixtures/small-clean/golden-standard.json is the single hand-authored target that all pipeline convergence work is measured against. It represents what the pipeline SHOULD produce — not what is fed into the pipeline. If it is wrong, every downstream improvement is optimising toward the wrong target.
The file currently defines an L4→L3→L2→L1 hierarchy with 16 items. It has no tests, validation, or schema — it is a free-form JSON with conventions enforced only by the author's intent.

There are already two competing hierarchy representations in the fixture folder: golden-standard.json (hand-authored, semantic, goal-state) and golden-hierarchy.json (an earlier reviewer pass that differs in how it groups files — e.g. it places package.json and src/index.js under an L3 called 'public library surface', whereas golden-standard.json groups them under separate L3s called 'scaffolding' and 'code'). These two do NOT agree on the intended grouping.

The golden-standard.json has several areas that need scrutiny: (1) L3 'scaffolding' contains only ONE L2 ('packaging') which contains only ONE L1 ('package.json') — is a 1-1-1 chain semantically justified? (2) The L3/L2 names are inconsistent in naming convention. (3) There is no explicit statement that tests are co-located intentionally. (4) Description quality is uneven. (5) No top-level schema or contract block.

The schema/field names in the golden-standard.json may evolve over time as we learn from more complex projects. The important thing is that the SEMANTIC CONTENT is correct and the structure is internally consistent for slug-ify right now.
features.acceptance:
- golden-standard.json and golden-hierarchy.json no longer disagree on which L3/L2 grouping is correct (one is updated to match the other, or one is removed).
- Every 1-child grouping has a justification in its description.
- No item description is tautological (e.g. 'This is the slugify feature.' is rejected).
- All item names follow one consistent convention.
- A top-level 'contract' or 'schema' field explains what level, name, description, children, dependencies mean.
- The file explicitly states that L0 and flows are out of scope.
- A developer with no prior context can read the file and correctly describe the slug-ify project structure.

features.title: Perform a full explanatory golden-standard contract audit and convergence pass
features.description: Run and preserve a full explanatory audit of the golden-standard pipeline against the documented graph-first contract, with enough detail that a future implementer can reproduce the reasoning and arrive at the same remediation decisions. The audit should trace each failing or suspicious area through implementation, fixtures, and docs; explain why the current behavior occurs; classify the mismatch; and recommend the safest convergence path. The intended output is not merely a list of broken tests, but a teachable, evidence-backed contract reconciliation that makes the required results inevitable: a trustworthy golden oracle, graph extraction that captures the key semantic edges, surface behavior that reflects graph-backed knowledge, and clear separation between implementation bugs and stale expectations.
features.plan: For each affected area—level generation/grouping, graph extraction, graph snapshot semantics, signals, flows, search/navigation, viewer surfaces, and optimization—verify the current implementation with direct code inspection, compare it to the hand-authored fixtures and the docs-backed contract, then record: current behavior, intended behavior, why the mismatch happens, classification, risks, and recommended next action. Where the docs and fixtures disagree, force an explicit contract decision instead of silently changing code or goldens. Keep the audit explanatory enough that future work can continue without re-discovering the same reasoning.
context: This story has accumulated verified mismatches across graph extraction, semantic grouping, search/navigation, optimization deltas, signal taxonomy, and flow semantics.

The useful work was not just identifying failures, but tracing each one back to code paths, fixture expectations, and docs-backed contract language so that every mismatch could be classified as a code defect, stale golden, docs drift, or a required product/contract decision.
A final explicit feature is needed so the same style of deep, evidence-driven audit can be repeated or completed until the system and its golden standard converge on one documented contract.
features.acceptance: The story contains a preserved feature describing a full evidence-driven audit/convergence pass, and a future implementer can use it to systematically reproduce the audit method, explain each mismatch, and converge code, docs, and golden fixtures on one explicit contract.
features.rejection: Do not reduce this work to test triage alone. Do not update code, docs, or goldens opportunistically without first establishing which artifact is currently authoritative for the specific behavior under review. Avoid vague summaries that omit the reasoning chain needed to justify the remediation choice.
